title: Stencil acrylic paint on air-dry clay
subtitle: Applying a repeating geometric or botanical pattern to sealed air-dry clay using a cut stencil
excerpt: A stencil gives a repeating pattern to an air-dry clay surface with clean, sharp edges. The clay is sealed first, then painted through the stencil with acrylic paint, then re-sealed. The technique works on flat slabs, rounded pots, and tiles. No kiln required.
sourceNotes: Stencil decoration technique derived from traditional decorative art practice adapted for air-dry clay surfaces.

glossaryTerms.definition: Air-dried but unfired clay. Must be bone-dry before stencilling.

content.text: Seal the surface before you stencil. Without a seal coat, acrylic paint soaks into air-dry clay and the edges blur. This is different from stencilling on paper or fabric. The sealer stops absorption. Paint then sits sharp-edged on top.

air-dry clay piece, sealed with two coats of acrylic sealant (allow to dry between coats). A commercial or hand-cut stencil: acetate, plastic sheet, or stencil card. Acrylic paint in two colours (a base colour and a stencil colour). A stiff stubby brush or a foam sponge applicator for stippling paint through the stencil. Low-tack masking tape to hold the stencil.
Apply a base coat of acrylic paint to the sealed clay surface. This gives the stencil colour somewhere to sit other than the raw sealant. Allow to dry fully: 30 minutes.
Position the stencil on the surface and secure the edges with low-tack masking tape. On a curved surface, cut the stencil to shorter lengths so it conforms without buckling.

Load the stiff brush or foam applicator with a small amount of acrylic paint: less paint than you think. Excess paint bleeds under the stencil edge and blurs the pattern. Dab off most of the paint onto a dry cloth before applying to the stencil.
Apply the paint through the stencil with a stippling motion: up-and-down vertical presses of the brush, not side-to-side strokes. Side strokes push paint under the stencil edges.
Lift one corner of the stencil to check coverage. Add more paint where needed. When satisfied, peel the stencil straight back from the surface: lift it upward and away cleanly, not at an angle.

Allow the stencilled paint to dry fully: 20 minutes. For repeating patterns, reposition and re-tape the stencil and repeat. Clean the stencil between repositions to prevent paint build-up transferring to the next section.
When all sections are complete and dry, apply one final coat of acrylic sealant over the entire piece to protect the stencilled design.
Paint bleeds under the stencil edge: too much paint on the applicator, or brush used with side strokes. Use less paint and stipple vertically.
Stencil lifts and shifts during application: masking tape not adhering on a curved surface. Use more tape points; cut the stencil into a smaller section that follows the curve more easily.
Paint absorbs into the clay and blurs even though it was stencilled: the sealant coat was applied to un-dried clay. The clay must be bone-dry before any sealant.

rows.cause: Paint layer too thin; stencil colour too close to the base colour in tone
rows.fix: Apply two stippling passes through the stencil, allowing each to dry slightly between. Increase the contrast between base and stencil colours.

rows.problem: Stencil stuck to the clay surface
rows.cause: Paint dried and bonded the stencil down
rows.fix: Lift slowly, peeling back at a very shallow angle. Dampen the edge with water to loosen. Next time, lift the stencil before the paint is fully dry.
